Local service between these facilities and the originators and receivers of traffic was ordinarily conducted over city streets within municipal confines or nearby suburban areas. This situation prevailed before the urban explosion that has characterized the past few decades. Technological advances in transportation have changed the urban structure. More specifically, the impact of the motor vehicle on the urban locational alignment of the users of transportation has been profound since the advent of our regulation of motor carriage. No longer dependent on rail and water facilities, business and industry has dispersed and located along freeways and transportation arteries skirting the city.
The significance of these observations is that the "intraterminal v. intercity or intercommunity" test no longer provides a complete and clear standard for delineating the geographic scope of the section 203(b)(8) exemption. The original concept is disappearing. Modern urban development is out of step with the previous pattern of a central business district with commerce and industry clustered around rail sidings. Whether it is attributed to "urban sprawl" or the "multi-nucleated" nature of modern cities, the use of terms such as intra- or intercity or intercommunity, without more, has lost much of value in describing the proper geographic limits of the commercial zone exemption.
